Re-read on 2026-10-08; the text is unchanged since the last seal. "A DPIA, or data protection impact assessment, is a written GDPR check of privacy risk before high-risk personal-data processing begins." is one whole sentence that expands the acronym and answers the query in its first words. It agrees with Article 35(1) GDPR (the gdpr-info.eu copy of the Regulation, read on 2026-10-08): where processing is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller carries out the assessment before the processing. The section moved onto this page under answer 17.7 does not touch the row.

Re-read on 2026-10-08; the text is unchanged since the last seal. Sentence 1, "A DPIA, or data protection impact assessment, is a written GDPR review completed before a company begins personal-data processing likely to carry high privacy risk.", agrees with Article 35(1) GDPR (assessment before the processing, where it is likely to result in a high risk; the gdpr-info.eu copy of the Regulation, read on 2026-10-08). Sentence 2, "It assesses what data the company collects, why, and how the company reduces that risk.", matches Article 35(7)(a) (a description of the processing and its purposes) and (d) (the measures envisaged to address the risks). Sentence 3, "It differs from a fairness review of the system's decision.", is the distinction from the AI Act assessment that the page's source list covers (Article 27), carried unchanged from the 2026-10-02 review. Re-read on 2026-10-08 against the gdpr-info.eu copy of Article 35 GDPR and the artificialintelligenceact.eu copy of Article 26 of the AI Act (both read on 2026-10-08); the text is unchanged since the last seal. The three situations are Article 35(3)(a) to (c): "large-scale profiling with legal or similarly significant effects" is the systematic and extensive evaluation based on automated processing, including profiling, with legal or similarly significant effects; "large-scale processing of special-category data, such as health or biometric records" is processing on a large scale of Article 9(1) data; "systematic large-scale monitoring of a public space" is systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area on a large scale. Paragraph 2 matches Article 35(7)(a) to (d) (description and necessity, risk to the people concerned, measures) and Article 35(2) (the controller seeks the data protection officer's advice, where one is designated, when carrying out the assessment; the row reads "while it carries out the assessment. Signing off afterward does not count."). Paragraph 3 matches Article 26(9) of the AI Act: deployers of high-risk systems use the information provided under Article 13 to comply with the Article 35 GDPR duty. The row does not say the three situations are the only ones. Article 35(3) says the assessment is required "in particular" in those cases, and Article 35(1) covers any processing likely to result in a high risk; the first sentence of the new section on monitoring staff says as much: Article 35(3) names three cases, and Article 35(1) asks for a DPIA wherever processing is likely to result in a high risk to people. Read the two together: the three situations in this row are the Article 35(3) cases, and the new sentence says they are not the only ones. Rider on the last sentence: "Most consequential AI systems land in the first of these by default." is the page's rule of thumb, not a count or a sourced finding; it was accepted on 2026-10-02 and the move does not touch it.

The article keeps one sentence and a link to this section and no longer carries the paragraph. Sentence map, old five sentences to the new text. (1) The opening sentence, which said the Article 29 Working Party's 2017 guidelines list systematic monitoring and data about vulnerable people among their criteria, was split: "Systematic monitoring is one." and "Data about vulnerable people is another" are its two halves. (2) The sentence that employees may count as vulnerable because of the power imbalance was merged into the end of the second half ("and employees may count as vulnerable because of the power imbalance"). (3) "Meeting two criteria means a DPIA in most cases." is verbatim. (4) The dashboard sentence was reworded from a usage dashboard to "Whether a dashboard of AI tool usage counts as systematic monitoring depends on how person-level it is." with the same claim. (5) "That is an inference, not a regulator's ruling." is verbatim and still sits on the dashboard sentence. Two things are new: the section's first paragraph, "Article 35(3) names three cases, but Article 35(1) asks for a DPIA wherever processing is likely to result in a high risk to people.", and the phrase "list criteria that point to high risk" that now opens the second paragraph. Verification of both additions. Article 35 GDPR, read in the gdpr-info.eu copy of the Regulation on 2026-10-08 and recorded in research record 06 (lines 213-214: "Article 35(1): a DPIA (data protection impact assessment) is required where processing is likely to result in high risk. 35(3) lists three cases."): paragraph 1 applies where processing "is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller shall, prior to the processing, carry out an assessment", and paragraph 3 says the assessment "shall in particular be required in the case of" three cases (an evaluation based on automated processing, including profiling, with legal or similarly significant effects; large-scale processing of special categories of data or of data on criminal convictions and offences; large-scale systematic monitoring of a publicly accessible area). So the new sentence is accurate: 35(3) names three cases and 35(1) is the general rule; "asks for" and "to people" are plain glosses of "shall ... carry out" and "rights and freedoms of natural persons". The phrase "criteria that point to high risk" rests on WP 248 rev.01, the page's own source for the criteria and the two-criteria rule, as record 06 reads it (lines 220-227): nine criteria, two criteria meaning a DPIA "in most cases", one criterion sometimes enough, with systematic monitoring and vulnerable data subjects among them and employees named as a group that "may include" vulnerable subjects. Criteria whose combination calls for a DPIA, which Article 35(1) ties to likely high risk, are indicators of high risk. The phrase is a plain description, not a quotation of WP 248. A search on 2026-10-08 of the copy of WP 248 rev.01 published by the Norwegian data protection authority (datatilsynet.no) returned the guidelines' passage that the more criteria a processing meets, the more likely it is to present a high risk to the rights and freedoms of data subjects and so to require a DPIA; that is the guidelines' own framing of the criteria as indicators of high risk. The full guidelines were not fetched that day (the fetch returned no file), so the nine criteria and the two-criteria rule rest on record 06. Neither addition is an owner fact, number, period, role or practice: the section has no first person, and its only numbers are the article numbers, the year 2017 and "two criteria", all from the sources. Retained hedges: "may count" for employees as vulnerable, "in most cases" for the two-criteria rule, and "an inference, not a regulator's ruling" on the dashboard question; none was dropped. Text tension for the parent, not a defect: the new first sentence sits beside the unchanged definition row ("in three situations"); the definition's three situations are the Article 35(3) cases and the new sentence says so with "but". The other two sections are unchanged and were re-read on 2026-10-08. That is why explaining the difference is usually the more useful answer than either document alone.") keeps the wording of the 2026-10-02 plain-language review (glossary.json#7), which changed phrasing only and added no claim. The section "What to do about it" keeps "Write the DPIA before the system is built, not after" (the one agentless passive left after that review) and "Start from what the system actually collects and why"; "Consult the data protection officer while there is time to act" agrees with Article 35(2), read on 2026-10-08: the controller "shall seek the advice of the data protection officer, where designated, when carrying out a data protection impact assessment". The link to the AI Governance Starter Kit resource is unchanged. Dropped from the earlier entry: the old date line and the description of a page without the moved section. Both additions restate sourced legal text (Article 35 GDPR and WP 248), not an owner answer, fact or practice.
